🚀 REVISION BLOCK (Sections 1–5)

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Why does a WebSocket tier need stickiness at all? The socket lives in one process; there's nothing to route to elsewhere. It's inherent, not configured.
How do you pick the heartbeat interval? Under half the smallest idle timeout on the path — ~20–25s behind a 60s ALB.
Default Linux TCP keepalive idle time? 7200s (2 hours) — useless as a liveness check.
What makes a reconnect resumable? A per-channel sequence number the client sends back, plus a bounded server-side buffer.
What's the guaranteed mass-disconnection event? Your own rolling deploy.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Third pass (day before) — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Running WebSocket is five problems the protocol doesn't solve. Connections pin to one process, so every message must find that process — that's the fan-out bus. Every box in the path has an idle timer, typically 60 seconds, so you need application ping/pong well inside it. Dead peers don't announce themselves, so liveness is your pong timeout. Reconnects need a sequence number and a bounded replay buffer or clients lose messages. And your own rolling deploy is the largest disconnection event you will ever have — it needs draining and jittered reconnect, or it looks exactly like an outage.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

What actually makes a WebSocket "sticky", and what does that break?

🎯 Really testing: whether you understand stickiness here is a property of the transport, not a load-balancer setting.

Stickiness in the HTTP sense — cookies, ip_hash — is a routing decision made per request. A WebSocket has exactly one request, the upgrade, and after that the TCP connection is the session. There's nothing left to route: the socket's file descriptor exists in one process on one node, so affinity is inherent and permanent for the connection's life. You don't enable it; you inherit it.

What it breaks is everything that assumed interchangeable backends. Autoscaling out doesn't relieve loaded nodes, because existing connections don't migrate. Scaling in disconnects everyone on the terminated node. Rolling deploys sever connections by design. Zonal failover isn't a re-route, it's a mass reconnect. And any per-user state you cached in that process — subscriptions, permissions, the last sequence number — is gone when the process is, so the honest design keeps that state derivable from somewhere else.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Redis pub/sub, consistent hashing, or a dedicated router for fan-out?

📍 Seen in the wild: the immediate follow-up once you've said "the gateway subscribes to a channel".

🎯 Really testing: whether you can see the amplification factor, not just name a technology.

Pub/sub is the default and the right first answer: every gateway subscribes to the channels its connections care about, publishers don't know or care where sockets live, and adding gateways requires no coordination. The cost is amplification — a message on a popular channel is delivered to every subscribing node, so bus load grows with messages × nodes, and a channel every user subscribes to means every message hits every node.

Consistent hashing inverts that: route by user or room id so a given channel lives on exactly one gateway, and a message crosses the network once. You've traded amplification for a rebalancing problem — a node joining or leaving reshuffles a fraction of keys, and during that window messages can land on the wrong node — plus hot-key risk, because one very popular room is now one node's problem.

The practical answer is usually pub/sub sharded by channel hash: gateways subscribe only to their shard of the keyspace, which bounds amplification to messages × nodes-per-shard while keeping the operational simplicity. I'd reach for a dedicated routing tier only when a single room's fan-out genuinely exceeds what one node can write.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

One client stops reading but doesn't disconnect. What happens?

📍 Seen in the wild: the slow-consumer probe — the failure mode people who've only read about WebSocket never mention.

The kernel send buffer fills first, then your write returns EAGAIN or blocks. What happens next is entirely your framework's choice, and the dangerous default is an unbounded userspace queue: the connection stays "healthy", the queue grows with every broadcast, and one stalled mobile client on a busy channel accumulates megabytes. A few thousand of those and the process OOMs — with idle CPU, normal message rates, and no errors anywhere. That's the signature: memory climbing on a subset of nodes with nothing else moving.

The fix is a bounded outbound queue per connection with an explicit policy when it fills: drop the connection (correct for chat and collaboration, where the client resumes by sequence number), drop oldest (correct for tickers, where only the latest value matters), or apply real backpressure to the source (correct when the source is a single stream you control). All three are defensible; having no policy is not. The metric to graph is p99 outbound queue depth, and it predicts the OOM by minutes.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

Design a zero-message-loss rollout for a 200k-connection gateway tier.

🎯 Really testing: whether you treat deploys as a designed traffic event rather than an infrastructure detail.

The highest-stakes constraint is that severing 200k sockets at once produces a reconnect wave larger than the tier's accept capacity, and the retry loop then keeps everyone out — the outage is self-inflicted and outlasts the deploy. So the rollout is shaped by how fast the tier can accept, not by how fast it can restart. If a node accepts ~2k connections/second and you're draining 20k at a time, each batch needs at least ten seconds of spread before the next.

The mechanism has three parts. The gateway stops accepting new connections and deregisters from the LB, but keeps existing ones alive for a drain window. It then sends an application-level "going away" frame carrying a server-chosen reconnect delay drawn from a jittered range, so clients disperse instead of synchronizing. Clients reconnect with their last sequence number per channel and the new node replays from a bounded buffer — which is what makes "zero loss" true rather than aspirational, since the buffer, not the connection, is the durability boundary.

The failure mode I'd monitor first is accept-queue depth during the rollout, with an automatic halt if it crosses a threshold. The deploy pipeline should be able to stop itself; a human noticing a reconnect storm at 3am is too late by an order of magnitude.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Fan-out approach Message crosses network Amplification Rebalance cost When you'd actually pick it
Pub/sub, all nodes subscribe once per node msgs × nodes none Default; small fleets, moderate rates
Pub/sub sharded by channel hash once per node-in-shard msgs × nodes/shards shard map change The usual production answer
Consistent hashing to one owner node once 1× keys reshuffle on membership change Very high message rates, tolerable rebalancing
Dedicated routing tier twice (router → gateway) 1× + a hop router is a scaling unit of its own One room's fan-out exceeds a single node

5. Memory Hook (Story Form)

Design axis: how much does the sender need to know about where the listener is sitting?

📖 Story — one message, four ways to reach the person holding the phone

  • Pub/sub to everyone. You shout the message into every room in the building; the room with the right person hears it, the other forty rooms hear it too and ignore it.

  • Sharded pub/sub. You shout only down the corridor that person's name belongs to. Fewer wasted rooms, and you only need to know the corridor.

  • Consistent hashing. You look up which room owns that name and walk straight there. Nobody else hears it — but when rooms are added, some names change room mid-sentence.

  • Dedicated router. You hand the message to a runner whose entire job is knowing where everyone sits. One extra hop, one place to keep correct.

🗺️ Story → Mechanism Mapping

  • shouting into every room = one publish delivered to every subscribing gateway process

  • "forty rooms ignore it" = the amplification factor messages × nodes

  • "names change room mid-sentence" = key reshuffle on membership change, and the window where messages land on the wrong owner

  • the runner = a routing tier that owns the connection registry and becomes its own scaling unit

📖 DEPTH BLOCK (Sections 6–19)

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The three numbers that size this tier

Heartbeat interval. interval < min(all idle timeouts on the path) / 2. Behind an ALB at 60s, 20–25s is the defensible choice; the factor of two means a single lost ping doesn't cost the connection. Detection time for a dead peer is interval + pong_timeout — about 35 seconds at 25/10, and that is the number to quote when asked how fast you notice a vanished client.

Fan-out amplification. Bus deliveries per second = publish_rate × subscribing_nodes. Twenty gateways and 5k messages/s on a broadly-subscribed channel is 100k deliveries/s at the bus — which is why sharding matters long before the gateways are stressed. Sharding into S shards divides this by S at the cost of a shard map every publisher must agree on.

Reconnect wave. C connections dropped, dispersed over a jitter window W, gives C/W connects per second against a tier that accepts A per second. Zero-loss requires W > C/A. Two hundred thousand connections against a fleet accepting 5k/s needs at least a 40-second dispersal window — and that inequality, not the restart time, is what sets the rollout schedule.

Where the timeouts actually live

Every hop has its own idle timer and they do not agree. A cloud L7 load balancer is commonly 60 seconds by default. nginx's proxy_read_timeout is 60 seconds and applies to the upgraded connection too. Carrier NAT entries for an idle TCP flow are often evicted around 30–60 seconds. Corporate proxies vary wildly and are usually the shortest. Linux TCP keepalive, meanwhile, starts probing after 7200 seconds — two hours — which is why it cannot be your liveness mechanism. The rule is to enumerate the path, take the minimum, and heartbeat under half of it.

7. Why It Matters in Production

The observable is concurrent connections and their churn rate, and the reason it matters is that this is the one tier where the failure modes are all quiet. A buffering proxy, a NAT eviction, a slow consumer, a half-open socket — none of them raise an error rate, none of them move latency percentiles, and all of them leave the connection count looking healthy while messages stop arriving.

The second reason is that this tier converts routine operations into traffic events. Everywhere else, a deploy is invisible; here it's the largest disconnection of the week. Autoscaling in is a disconnection. A zonal failover is a disconnection. Owning a WebSocket tier means owning a permanent obligation to make mass reconnection survivable, and teams that skip that discover it during their first incident rather than their first design review.

8. Command / Config / Code Example

# K8s: the four settings that decide whether a rollout is a deploy or an incident
spec:
  strategy:
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 1          # one gateway at a time; each is ~20k sockets
      maxSurge: 1
  minReadySeconds: 60            # let reconnects land before touching the next node
  template:
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 120   # MUST exceed drain window + jitter spread
      containers:
        - name: ws-gateway
          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              exec:
                # deregister first, then send "going away" with a jittered delay, then idle out
                command: ["/bin/sh","-c","/app/drain.sh --window 90s --reconnect-jitter 30s"]

# Is a heartbeat actually flowing? Count socket states on a gateway node.
ss -tan state established '( sport = :8443 )' | wc -l     # live sockets on this node
ss -tan state close-wait  '( sport = :8443 )' | wc -l     # peer closed, app hasn't — a leak indicator
cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_keepalive_time                  # 7200 — why you cannot rely on it

9. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

Scenario: 200k connections across 10 gateways (20k each), the rollout above, one node at a time.

🚀 [0s]  drain.sh on node-3: deregister from target group → LB stops sending new upgrades
    │
    ▼
📡 [2s]  node-3 broadcasts {"type":"going_away","reconnect_after_ms":random(0,30000)}
    │      to its 20,000 sockets
    ▼
🔄 [2–32s] clients close and reconnect, dispersed over 30s → ~667 connects/s
    │      spread across 9 remaining nodes = ~74/s each. Accept capacity ~2k/s/node. ✅
    ▼
💾 [3–33s] each reconnect sends last seq per channel; new node LRANGEs the room buffer
    │      and replays the 0–3 messages missed. Median gap measured: 1.9s
    ▼
❌ [33s] ~140 clients (0.7%) haven't reconnected — backgrounded tabs, asleep, offline
    │
    ▼
⏱️ [90s] drain window ends, node-3 force-closes the stragglers and exits
    │
    ▼
✅ [150s] minReadySeconds satisfied, node-4 begins. Total rollout ≈ 25 min for 10 nodes.

1. Deregistering before broadcasting is the ordering that matters. Reverse it and clients reconnect into the node you're about to kill, which turns one disconnection into two. The LB must stop sending upgrades before the node tells anyone to go.

2. The jitter window is computed, not guessed. 20k connections over 30 seconds is 667/s against ~18k/s of remaining accept capacity — comfortable. Drop the jitter to zero and it's 20,000 connects in one second, which overruns the accept queues, produces connection resets, and triggers client retry loops that make the next node's drain worse. This is the inequality from Section 6 doing its job.

3. The replay buffer is what makes the gap invisible, not the speed of reconnect. A 1.9-second median gap would lose messages without it. The buffer's retention has to exceed the worst reconnect gap you tolerate, not the median — which is why 5 minutes is a common choice against a 30-second jitter window.

4. The 0.7% stragglers are the honest part of the answer. Backgrounded and sleeping clients won't reconnect on your schedule at all, so terminationGracePeriodSeconds has to exceed the drain window or Kubernetes kills the pod mid-drain and those clients get an abrupt close instead of a graceful one. They resume by sequence number when they wake — which is exactly why sequence-number resume is worth building.

5. Twenty-five minutes for a rollout is the real cost. One node at a time with a 60-second settle is slow, and shortening it means raising the reconnect rate. That trade — deploy speed against reconnect pressure — is the operational signature of this tier, and it's worth stating out loud because it's the thing nobody budgets for.

10. When TO Use This

  • You already committed to WebSocket for a genuinely bidirectional product — this note is the bill, and none of it is optional once the sockets exist.

  • Any long-lived connection tier at all, including SSE at scale: stickiness, idle timeouts, heartbeats, replay buffers and reconnect storms apply identically. Only the framing differs.

  • When designing a rollout for a stateful edge — the drain-and-disperse pattern here generalizes to any tier where clients hold a connection rather than making requests.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Don't build stickiness-aware infrastructure for one-way traffic. If the answer is SSE, you still get the idle-timeout and reconnect problems, but you get browser-managed reconnect and Last-Event-ID for free — a materially smaller bill for the same delivery.

  • Don't use unbounded outbound queues, ever. "We'll buffer whatever the client hasn't read" is a memory-exhaustion bug with a delay fuse. Bound it and choose a policy.

  • Don't rely on connection count as a health signal. It's the metric that stays green through every quiet failure in this domain. Client-observed delivery lag is the SLI; connection count is capacity.

  • Don't shard by user id when the fan-out unit is a room. You'll deliver every room message to every node holding one of its members, which is the amplification you sharded to avoid. Shard by the channel, not the subscriber.

  • Don't attempt zero-downtime connection migration. Moving a live socket between processes is a research project; the working pattern is fast, cheap, resumable reconnection. Aim for a 2-second invisible gap, not a 0-second one.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Enable sticky sessions on the load balancer and WebSocket scaling is solved."

✅ Reality: Stickiness is automatic — the TCP connection is the session. The unsolved problems are fan-out to the node holding the socket, replay across reconnects, and what a deploy does to 200k of them. The LB setting isn't part of any of that.

❌ Misconception: "TCP keepalive will detect dead clients."

✅ Reality: Linux defaults to probing after 7200 seconds. Two hours of holding a dead session's memory and subscriptions. Application ping/pong at 20–25 seconds is the only mechanism that detects it in a useful window.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): I assumed a reconnect storm was a capacity problem you solved by over-provisioning. It's a dispersal problem — the peak is C/W, and widening W with jitter is far cheaper than raising accept capacity. The server telling clients when to come back is the highest-leverage control in this whole tier, and it costs one field in a close frame.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Naming Redis pub/sub and stopping. It's the right first answer and incomplete without the amplification factor. Say messages × nodes, then say how you'd shard it — that's the difference between having read a diagram and having operated one.

Describing reconnect without describing resume. Reconnecting is trivial; not losing the messages that fired during the gap is the design. Sequence numbers, a bounded buffer, and a retention window are the answer, and "we re-fetch full state on connect" is an acceptable alternative if you say it deliberately.

Skipping the slow consumer. Almost nobody volunteers it, and it's the failure that actually takes the tier down — quietly, with idle CPU. Raising it unprompted is one of the strongest signals in this topic.

Treating deploys as out of scope. The largest disconnection event in the system is scheduled and self-inflicted. An answer that covers network failures but not rollouts has skipped the common case.

Quoting a heartbeat interval with no path enumeration. "We ping every 30 seconds" is meaningless without the smallest idle timeout on the path. Derive the number: enumerate the hops, take the minimum, halve it.

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Metric Value Context Source
AWS ALB idle timeout default 60s Applies to WebSocket and SSE alike; raise it, don't rely on it AWS ELB docs
nginx proxy_read_timeout default 60s Applies to the upgraded connection nginx docs
Linux tcp_keepalive_time default 7200s Why TCP keepalive is not a liveness check Linux tcp(7)
Control frame payload cap 125 bytes Ping/pong payloads must fit unfragmented RFC 6455 §5.5
Practical heartbeat interval 20–25s Under half of a 60s path minimum Derived from the above
Dead-peer detection time interval + pong timeout (~35s) The number to quote when asked Derived
Full Jitter for reconnect random(0, min(cap, base·2^n)) Beat plain and equal jitter on total work and completion time AWS Architecture Blog

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⏱️ Latency Sharded fan-out cuts bus load but adds a shard-map lookup and a rebalancing window where delivery can be misrouted
💰 Cost The tier is sized by peak concurrent connections, not by traffic, so it costs the same at 3am as at peak
🔒 Security / visibility Frames are opaque to the WAF and L7 rate limiter, so abuse controls move into the application and must be built per message type
📈 Scale Adding nodes helps only new connections; relieving a hot node requires disconnecting people
🔧 Ops complexity Every deploy, scale-in and failover becomes a designed traffic event with its own runbook
🐛 Debuggability The characteristic failures are all silent — no errors, no latency change; you must instrument delivery lag client-side or you cannot see them

16. Real World Usage

Chat and collaboration platforms run exactly this shape: a thin gateway tier holding sockets, a sharded bus for fan-out, and a document or message service that owns durable state. The public engineering writeups from that space consistently identify connection churn during deploys — not steady-state load — as the hard problem.

Live sports and betting platforms hit the fan-out extreme: a single event channel with millions of subscribers, where amplification forces a dedicated routing tier and often a CDN-style edge fan-out rather than pub/sub at all.

Realtime AI voice products combine the worst of both: a bidirectional audio stream per session (so no SSE escape hatch) plus expensive per-session GPU state, which makes a severed connection costly enough that resume-by-sequence and long drain windows stop being optional.

17. Acronym Decoder

Topic name is not an acronym.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

  • 27-keepalives-idle-timeouts.md — where the 60-second defaults come from

  • 74-choosing-realtime-transport.md — whether you needed this tier at all

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • SSE with Last-Event-ID — the same operational problems with browser-managed reconnect and resume included

  • Platform push (APNs/FCM) — no connection to operate; the right answer for backgrounded mobile

  • Managed realtime services — buy the connection tier rather than run it; you trade cost and lock-in for not owning this note

🧩 Composes with (used together in real systems)

  • Consistent hashing — the sharding primitive behind channel-owner routing

  • Connection draining and preStop hooks — how the rollout becomes gradual rather than instantaneous

  • Cross-folder: K8s rollout strategy and HPA behaviour for long-lived connections → Section 13; retry/backoff discipline → 68-timeouts-retries-backoff.md

19. System Design Application

How this concept appears in a system design tech discussion

Once you've chosen WebSocket in a design round, this is the rest of the round. Expect "how does a message get to the right server", "what happens when you deploy", and "what happens when one client stops reading" in some order. The strong answer keeps the connection tier deliberately dumb, puts durability in a buffer rather than in the connection, and treats the rollout as a rate-limited traffic event with a computed dispersal window.

Topology diagram

Capacity / cost back-of-envelope

Scale Constraint Solution
200k connections Accept rate during rollout; per-node fds and heap 10 nodes × 20k, jittered 30s dispersal, minReadySeconds ≥ drain window
2M connections Bus amplification msgs × nodes; replay buffer memory Shard pub/sub by channel hash; cap buffer length per channel, not just TTL
20M connections Single-region tier and single bus saturate; cross-region reconnect Regional tiers with regional buses; global routing by user home region; accept a partition-tolerant delivery model

Where this typically breaks at scale

  • At 10x, the bus saturates before the gateways do, and the symptom is delivery lag on the busiest channels only — easy to misread as an application bug.

  • At 100x, replay buffers dominate memory: every active channel holds its recent history, and the TTL that was fine at 200k is a multi-terabyte working set.

  • Operationally, the 3am version is a scale-in event during a traffic dip: the autoscaler terminates two nodes with no drain, 40k clients reconnect simultaneously into a shrunken fleet, and the tier scales out again — after the incident.

Monitoring & SLOs

  • Client-observed delivery lag, p50/p99 — the SLI. Everything else in this tier can look healthy while this degrades.

  • Outbound queue depth per connection, p99 — the slow-consumer detector; alert before the OOM, not after.

  • Accept-queue depth and connect-error rate during rollouts — the deploy circuit breaker; wire it to halt the rollout automatically.

  • Pong-timeout rate and connection churn — a step change means a middlebox timeout changed or a node is unhealthy; a steady rise means something is severing connections quietly.

  • Bus deliveries per second vs publishes per second — the amplification ratio, graphed directly, so sharding decisions are made on data rather than instinct.

📋 Table/playbook topic. Section 4 is the centrepiece and sits above Section 3. Section 5 is omitted, Section 6 is discharged by the decision flowchart, and Section 9 is a set of worked decisions rather than a packet trace.

📚 Reference Links

  • SSE semantics (normative) — WHATWG HTML §9.2: Server-sent events

  • WebSocket semantics (normative) — RFC 6455

  • HTTP/2 streams and flow control — RFC 9113 §5 and §6.9

  • gRPC's four call types — grpc.io: Core concepts, architecture and lifecycle

  • Bonus — hpbn.co: WebSocket · Server-Sent Events

🚀 REVISION BLOCK

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
First question you ask, before any protocol name? Does the client stream continuously? Everything follows from the direction.
Only option a browser can't reach without a proxy? gRPC — browsers need gRPC-Web plus a translating proxy.
Which two multiplex over one connection natively? HTTP/2 streaming and gRPC (which is HTTP/2). SSE does too, since it is an h2 stream.
Which one has no framing and makes you invent it? Raw HTTP chunked streaming — no records, no event names, no ids.
The tiebreak when two options both work? Pick the one that stays inside HTTP, so auth, WAF, rate limits and tracing keep working.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Third pass (day before) — re-read Section 4 alone.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Four transports, one decision, and it isn't made on capability — WebSocket can do everything the others can, which is exactly why choosing it first is the wrong instinct. Ask three questions in order. Does the client stream continuously, or does it just listen? Is the consumer a browser or another service? Do you need a schema and codegen across teams? One-way to a browser is SSE. Two-way to a browser is WebSocket. Service-to-service with a contract is gRPC. And plain chunked HTTP is enough more often than people admit.

4. Quick Comparison Table — the centrepiece

The full matrix

SSE WebSocket HTTP/2 streaming (chunked / h2 stream) gRPC streaming
Direction server → client full duplex server → client per request (client-stream via request body) all four: unary, server-stream, client-stream, bidi
Underlying protocol HTTP (any version) own protocol after 101; h2 via RFC 8441 HTTP/1.1 chunked or an h2 stream HTTP/2 only
Payload UTF-8 text only text or binary anything protobuf (binary)
Framing given to you records, blank-line delimited, named events, ids frames with opcodes none — you invent it length-prefixed messages, typed
Schema / codegen none none none first-class: .proto → clients in every language
Browser-reachable native EventSource native WebSocket native (fetch + ReadableStream) ❌ needs gRPC-Web + proxy
Reconnect & resume automatic, Last-Event-ID you build all of it you build all of it you build it; deadlines are first-class
Multiplexing yes, over h2 no (one connection), yes with RFC 8441 yes, native yes, native
Backpressure signal h2 flow control only none at the app layer h2 flow control flow control surfaced in the API
Survives ordinary proxies usually (unless they buffer) often not (Upgrade stripped) usually needs h2 end-to-end
Observability with existing tools full — it's HTTP poor after 101 full needs gRPC-aware tooling
Ops weight low high low medium
When you'd actually pick it one-way text push to a browser: tokens, feeds, progress client is a continuous producer: audio, cursors, input you own both ends and want no ceremony service-to-service with a shared contract

The decision, as a flowchart

The three questions, in order

  1. Direction. Does the client produce a continuous stream, or only consume one? This eliminates half the matrix immediately and is the question people skip.

  2. Consumer type. Browser or service? Browsers can't speak gRPC without a translating proxy; services don't need EventSource's conveniences and usually do want a schema.

  3. Contract. Do multiple teams or languages consume this? A .proto with generated clients is worth real operational weight; a single frontend team consuming JSON is not.

Tiebreak when two options both work: choose the one that stays inside HTTP. Auth middleware, WAF rules, per-route rate limits, access logs and trace propagation are worth more than a few bytes per message.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

What does gRPC streaming give you that HTTP/2 streaming doesn't, given gRPC is HTTP/2?

🎯 Really testing: whether you know the layers, or think gRPC is a different transport.

Nothing at the transport layer — gRPC streams are HTTP/2 streams, with content-type: application/grpc and length-prefixed messages in the body. Everything gRPC adds sits above that: a typed schema with generated clients, four defined call shapes, deadlines that propagate as a header and are enforced end-to-end, status codes richer than HTTP's, interceptors, and flow control surfaced into the API instead of hidden in the connection.

The practical consequence is that "should we use HTTP/2 streaming or gRPC streaming?" is really "do we want a contract and codegen, and are we willing to run h2 end-to-end and gRPC-aware tooling to get it?" If both ends are yours and one team owns them, raw chunked responses are less machinery for the same bytes. Across teams and languages, the schema is the point.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Your product streams LLM tokens down and takes live audio up. One transport or two?

📍 Seen in the wild: the voice-agent design round, and the best question in this topic because both answers are defensible.

🎯 Really testing: whether you'll split by traffic shape or reflexively unify.

Two transports is the honest default. Audio up is continuous, binary and latency-critical — WebSocket or WebRTC. Tokens down are text, resumable, and benefit from Last-Event-ID and every piece of HTTP infrastructure you already own. Splitting means the expensive, hard-to-operate channel only carries the traffic that actually needs it.

One transport wins when the two directions are correlated in time — barge-in, where the user interrupting must cancel generation within tens of milliseconds. Coordinating that across two connections means a cancellation racing down a second path, and a WebSocket carrying both directions makes ordering trivial. That's a real argument, and it's the one voice products usually land on.

So: split when the directions are independent, unify when interruption semantics couple them. What I wouldn't accept is unifying "for consistency" — that's paying WebSocket's operational bill on the token path for no return.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

Which of these survives contact with the middle of the internet, and how do you find out before launch?

📍 Seen in the wild: the question that separates people who've shipped to enterprise customers.

Ranked by survival: HTTP chunked and SSE pass almost everywhere, because they're ordinary responses — the failure mode isn't rejection but buffering, where a proxy holds the body and delivers it at the end. WebSocket is next and fails harder: an intermediary that strips Upgrade/Connection returns 200 or 400 instead of 101, with no useful diagnostic. gRPC is the most fragile, needing HTTP/2 with prior knowledge or ALPN end to end; any hop that downgrades to 1.1 breaks it entirely, which is why gRPC-Web and its proxy exist.

You find out by testing from the networks your users are on, not from your laptop. Two probes cover most of it: curl -N against the streaming endpoint to see whether bytes dribble or arrive in one lump, and a raw curl -i upgrade request to see whether a 101 comes back. Run both from a corporate VPN, a mobile tether and a customer's guest network. The failure presents as "works for us, broken for that one enterprise account" — which is a middlebox until proven otherwise.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

One product, three consumers: a browser app, a partner's backend, and a mobile client. What do you expose?

🎯 Really testing: whether you'll expose one transport per consumer type or invent a lowest-common-denominator that suits none of them.

The highest-stakes constraint is that these three consumers have different capabilities and different contracts, so a single transport is a compromise imposed on all of them. The design I'd defend is one core event stream internally, with three edges: SSE for the browser, gRPC server-streaming (or a webhook, if the partner prefers push-to-them) for the partner backend, and platform push plus a resume-on-foreground fetch for mobile.

The composition is what makes it cheap: one internal publish path writes to a durable ordered log; each edge adapter is a thin translator holding connections and converting the log's cursor into that transport's resume mechanism — Last-Event-ID for SSE, a stream offset for gRPC, a since parameter for the mobile catch-up call. Nothing about the event source knows which transports exist.

The failure mode I'd monitor first is divergence between edges: the same event delivered at materially different lag on different transports, which is how "the web app shows it but the API doesn't" incidents start. One lag metric, tagged by edge, on one dashboard.

📖 DEPTH BLOCK

6. Mechanism & Math

Conditional section, satisfied by the decision flowchart in Section 4 — this topic is a selection framework, and the underlying mechanisms are covered in full by 71-server-sent-events.md, 72-websocket.md and Section 6 of the HTTP-versions folder.

One number is worth carrying, because it's the one people guess at: per-message overhead. WebSocket adds 2–14 bytes of frame header. SSE adds data: plus a trailing blank line — about 8 bytes, plus any id:/event: fields you emit. gRPC adds a 5-byte length prefix per message on top of HTTP/2 framing, and its protobuf payload is typically much smaller than the equivalent JSON. At a hundred messages per second these differences are invisible; at a hundred thousand they decide the design. Ask for the message rate before letting anyone argue overhead.

7. Why It Matters in Production

The observable this decision moves is how many of your existing controls keep working. Choosing SSE or chunked HTTP means auth middleware, WAF rules, per-route rate limits, access logs and trace headers apply unchanged. Choosing WebSocket means each of those needs a replacement or an exemption, and every exemption is a line item in a security review. Choosing gRPC means your entire observability stack needs to speak gRPC.

The second thing it moves is who gets paged and how often. The transports differ far more in operational weight than in performance: connection tiers, heartbeats, reconnect storms and slow-consumer handling are permanent obligations, and they arrive with WebSocket regardless of how well it performs. Picking the lightest transport that meets the requirement is not conservatism — it's declining to buy an on-call burden you don't need.

9. Worked Decisions (the trace, for a table topic)

Scenario 1 — "Stream completions to our web chat UI." Checks: direction is server→client only; consumer is a browser; payload is text. → SSE. Defence: it's plain HTTP, so the existing auth and edge apply, and reconnect with Last-Event-ID is free. The thing to verify before shipping is that nothing on the path buffers.

Scenario 2 — "Live transcription: mic audio up, text down, with barge-in." Checks: the client streams continuously; payload up is binary; interruption couples the directions. → WebSocket for both directions. Defence: audio up rules out SSE, and barge-in makes ordering across two connections a race worth avoiding. Accept the operational bill knowingly — heartbeats, resume, drain-aware deploys.

Scenario 3 — "Our recommendation service should stream results to twelve internal callers in four languages." Checks: no browser; multiple teams and languages; a contract matters. → gRPC server-streaming. Defence: the .proto is the interface, deadlines propagate, and codegen removes twelve hand-written clients. Verify h2 survives every hop, including the mesh sidecars.

Scenario 4 — "Tail deployment logs in our internal admin tool." Checks: one-way; browser; text; both ends ours; nobody needs event names or replay. → Plain chunked HTTP with fetch + ReadableStream, or SSE if you want ids for free. Defence: the ceremony of any richer option buys nothing here. This is the scenario where the honest answer is the boring one.

Scenario 5 — "A partner wants our events." Checks: consumer is a backend you don't operate; they may be behind a firewall; delivery must survive their downtime. → Not a streaming transport at all — webhooks with retries, or a queue. Defence: a long-lived connection to a system you don't control converts their outage into your buffer-management problem. This is the scenario that catches people who've locked onto "which streaming protocol".

10. When TO Use This Framework

  • At the start of any realtime design round — running the three questions out loud takes twenty seconds and prevents the whole discussion from anchoring on WebSocket.

  • When someone proposes changing transports — the framework forces the argument onto direction, consumer and contract rather than on performance intuitions.

  • When a product has multiple consumer types — it's the tool that gets you to per-edge transports instead of a lowest-common-denominator compromise.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Not when the requirement is durability, not liveness. If missed messages are unacceptable and the consumer may be offline, none of these four is the answer — a queue or webhook delivery with retries is. Streaming transports deliver to whoever is listening.

  • Not when a managed realtime service is cheaper than the tier you're designing. Below a certain scale, the operational cost of a connection tier exceeds the vendor bill, and "buy it" is the architecturally honest answer.

  • Not as a substitute for measuring. The framework picks the shape; message rate, payload size and client network conditions decide the details, and those need numbers.

  • Not when the real constraint is your edge. If your CDN buffers responses and can't be configured otherwise, the transport decision has already been made for you — find that out first.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "WebSocket is the general-purpose choice because it can do everything the others can."

✅ Reality: Capability is the least important axis. WebSocket costs sticky routing, heartbeats, reconnect-and-resume, an opaque channel for your security stack, and a rollout that severs every session. Paying that for one-way traffic is the single most common mistake in this topic.

❌ Misconception: "gRPC streaming is a different, faster transport than HTTP/2 streaming."

✅ Reality: gRPC streams are HTTP/2 streams. What you're choosing is a schema, codegen, deadlines and typed statuses — an application-layer contract, not a faster wire.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): I treated "browser-reachable" as a footnote. It's the highest-order bit after direction — it eliminates gRPC outright unless you're prepared to run gRPC-Web and a translating proxy, and it's the constraint most likely to invalidate a design that otherwise looked clean.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Leading with a protocol name. The answer starts with direction, consumer and contract. Naming SSE or WebSocket before establishing those reads as pattern-matching, and the follow-up will expose it.

Ignoring the middle. All four work perfectly between two endpoints you control. What differs is survival through CDNs, corporate proxies and load balancers, and that's where the real risk sits. An answer that never mentions a proxy is describing a lab.

Confusing gRPC with a transport choice. Saying "gRPC is faster than REST" invites the question of what layer you think you're comparing. The honest framing is protobuf plus HTTP/2 plus a contract, and the contract is usually the reason.

Forgetting the browser can't speak gRPC. It's a hard constraint that people discover mid-implementation. Stating it early is a fast credibility win.

Recommending one transport for consumers with different capabilities. A browser app, a partner backend and a mobile client have genuinely different needs, and forcing one transport on all three produces a design that's mediocre for each. Per-edge adapters over a shared event source is the stronger answer.

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Metric Value Context Source
WebSocket frame header 2–14 bytes Per message, plus 4-byte mask client→server RFC 6455 §5.2
SSE per-record overhead ~8 bytes + optional id:/event: data: prefix and the terminating blank line WHATWG HTML §9.2
gRPC message prefix 5 bytes 1 compression flag + 4-byte length, above h2 framing grpc.io docs
HTTP/2 initial flow-control window 65,535 octets Per stream and per connection — the backpressure ceiling for SSE and gRPC alike RFC 9113 §6.9
Browser connections per origin (HTTP/1.1) 6 Caps concurrent SSE streams unless you're on h2 hpbn.co
WebSocket over h2 extended CONNECT + :protocol Needs support at every hop RFC 8441
gRPC call types 4 Unary, server-streaming, client-streaming, bidirectional grpc.io docs

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⏱️ Latency All four are sub-millisecond at the framing layer; real differences come from connection setup and buffering hops, not protocol overhead
💰 Cost SSE and chunked HTTP cost connections; WebSocket costs connections plus an operations team's attention; gRPC costs an h2-clean network path
🔒 Security / visibility SSE, chunked and gRPC keep HTTP-level controls (gRPC needs aware tooling); WebSocket goes opaque after 101
📈 Scale h2-based options multiplex onto one connection per client; WebSocket adds a connection and pins it for life
🔧 Ops complexity Ordered lightest to heaviest: chunked HTTP < SSE < gRPC < WebSocket. This ordering is the framework's real content
🐛 Debuggability curl -N reads SSE and chunked directly; gRPC needs grpcurl; WebSocket needs a protocol-aware client and usually in-app logging

16. Real World Usage

LLM provider APIs converged on HTTP + SSE for completions, and that convergence is itself the argument: one-way text with a resume point, delivered over infrastructure everyone already runs.

Voice and realtime AI products are the visible exception, running WebSocket precisely because audio flows upward continuously and interruption couples the two directions.

Internal service meshes run gRPC streaming for the same reason large organizations adopt protobuf at all — the schema is a coordination tool between teams, and streaming call types come along with it rather than being chosen separately.

17. Acronym Decoder

SSE — Server-Sent Events: the name states the direction constraint, which is the first question in the framework. gRPC — the "g" is famously recursive and teaches nothing; what matters is RPC: remote procedure call, i.e. a typed function call over the network, which is why a schema comes with it rather than being optional.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

  • 70-four-options.md — the polling/long-polling half of the decision space

  • 71-server-sent-events.md and 72-websocket.md — the two mechanisms this framework chooses between most often

  • 04-l4-vs-l7.md — why the boxes in the middle determine what survives

  • Section 10, Item 100 — the wider API choice framework, of which this is the streaming column

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • Webhooks — when the consumer is a backend you don't operate

  • Message queues and event streams — when durability, not liveness, is the requirement

  • WebRTC data channels — when you need peer-to-peer, or unreliable/unordered delivery for latency

🧩 Composes with (used together in real systems)

  • One internal event log with per-edge adapters — the pattern that lets different consumers get different transports

  • HTTP/2 — the substrate that makes SSE and gRPC multiplex, and quietly removes SSE's connection cap

  • Cross-folder: MCP transports (stdio / HTTP+SSE / streamable HTTP) → Item 99 in Section 10; streaming RAG responses → RAG folder §9

The queue is full. Block, drop, or disconnect?
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • HTTP/2 flow control and WINDOW_UPDATE — RFC 9113 §6.9

  • Backpressure, queuing strategies, high water mark — MDN: Streams API concepts

  • The practitioner's treatment, with the failure modes — Node.js: Backpressuring in Streams

  • Load shedding when you can't slow the producer — Google SRE Book: Handling Overload

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
HTTP/2's default flow-control window? 65,535 octets, per stream and per connection; consumers extend it with WINDOW_UPDATE.
Does WebSocket have application-layer backpressure? No. TCP's window is all you get; anything above it is your own queue and your own policy.
The three policies when a queue fills? Block the producer, drop messages (oldest or newest), or disconnect the consumer.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Backpressure is the consumer's ability to tell the producer to slow down. TCP has it — the receive window — and HTTP/2 adds a second layer with a 65,535-octet default per stream that the consumer extends with WINDOW_UPDATE. WebSocket has neither at the application layer, so a client that stops reading fills the kernel send buffer and then whatever queue your framework keeps, and the connection looks perfectly healthy while memory climbs. The design decision isn't whether to have a queue — it's what happens when it fills, and "grow" is not an answer.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Where does backpressure actually come from in an SSE or WebSocket path?

The bottom layer is TCP. A slow reader stops draining its receive buffer, its advertised window shrinks to zero, and the sender's kernel stops accepting bytes — at which point your write() returns EAGAIN or blocks. That signal is real and it is the only one WebSocket gives you, because the protocol has no window, no credit and no acknowledgement above the frame.

On HTTP/2 there's a second layer, and it's the one worth naming. Each stream and the connection as a whole start with a 65,535-octet window; the sender may not exceed it until the receiver sends WINDOW_UPDATE. That means an SSE stream or a gRPC call has genuine per-stream backpressure that doesn't stall the other streams sharing the connection — one slow consumer doesn't block its neighbours, which is exactly what HTTP/1.1 couldn't do.

The gap most systems fall into sits above both: your application writes into a userspace queue before the socket, so the TCP signal is absorbed by your own buffer. Backpressure only reaches your producer if you propagate it deliberately.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

The queue is full. Block, drop, or disconnect?

Blocking is correct when the producer can actually slow down and every message matters — reading from a file, a paginated database cursor, a model generating tokens you can pause. It's wrong the moment the producer is shared, because one slow consumer now throttles everyone: a broadcast loop that blocks on the slowest socket has converted one bad client into a global stall.

Dropping is correct when only the latest value matters — price ticks, telemetry, presence, cursor positions. Drop-oldest keeps the queue fresh and is almost always the right variant; drop-newest keeps history you no longer care about. The trade is explicit data loss for bounded memory and unaffected fast consumers.

Disconnecting is correct when the client can resume: chat, collaboration, anything with a sequence number and a replay buffer. It converts an unbounded memory problem into a bounded reconnect, and the client comes back and catches up. My default for a fan-out tier is a bounded queue with drop-oldest for lossy channels and disconnect-and-resume for ordered ones — and the queue depth graphed at p99, because that metric predicts an OOM minutes before it happens.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Transport Backpressure signal available What you must build
TCP (any) receive window → EAGAIN/blocking write Handle the write error rather than queueing past it
HTTP/2 stream (SSE, gRPC) per-stream + per-connection window, WINDOW_UPDATE Propagate the stall to the producer; don't buffer ahead of it
WebSocket none above TCP The whole policy: bounded queue, drop or disconnect
Message queue (Kafka, SQS) consumer pull rate, lag as a metric Alerting on lag; the queue itself absorbs the mismatch

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

Two numbers make this concrete. Time to exhaustion for an unbounded queue is available_memory / (message_size × produce_rate × slow_consumers) — at 2 KB messages, 500 messages/s and 200 stalled clients, that's 200 MB/s, so a 16 GB process dies in about eighty seconds. Queue sizing follows from how long a consumer may stall before you act: a high water mark of produce_rate × tolerated_stall and nothing more, because any depth beyond that is memory you're spending to delay a decision you've already made.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Don't apply blocking backpressure to a shared producer. One slow consumer stalling a broadcast loop is a self-inflicted outage; per-consumer queues with per-consumer policies exist precisely to isolate that.

  • Don't buffer ahead of the socket to "smooth" delivery. Your userspace queue absorbs the TCP signal, so the producer never learns anything is wrong — the system feels fine right up until it OOMs.

  • Don't use backpressure where you needed a queue. If the consumer can be offline for minutes, the right component is a broker with durable storage and a lag metric, not a bigger in-process buffer.

  • Don't ignore it on the read side. A client that streams audio faster than you can process it fills your receive path; the same three policies apply in the other direction, and the failure is usually blamed on the model or the disk.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "TCP handles backpressure, so my WebSocket server is fine."

✅ Reality: TCP's window stops the kernel from accepting more bytes. If your application queues into userspace before writing, that signal never reaches your producer — you've built an unbounded buffer in front of a working flow-control mechanism and disabled it.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): I read HTTP/2's flow control as a performance tuning knob. It's a correctness mechanism — the 65,535-octet default is why one slow SSE consumer doesn't stall the other streams on the same connection, and raising it without thinking trades exactly that isolation for throughput.

notes.title: WebTransport
notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The web API — W3C: WebTransport

  • The wire protocol (still an IETF draft) — draft-ietf-webtrans-http3: WebTransport over HTTP/3

🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What transport does it run on? QUIC, as an HTTP/3 session — not TCP, not a WebSocket upgrade.
The one thing WebSocket cannot do that it can? Unreliable, unordered delivery (datagrams) alongside reliable streams, on one connection.
Standardisation status? W3C API plus an IETF draft — shipping in some browsers, not yet an RFC.

Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

WebTransport is the QUIC-native successor to WebSocket: a browser API for a bidirectional session carrying both reliable ordered streams — several, independently multiplexed — and unreliable datagrams, over one HTTP/3 connection. It exists because of head-of-line blocking. WebSocket rides one TCP connection, so a lost segment stalls every message behind it, and there is no way to say "this frame is latency-critical, drop it rather than retransmit it". QUIC fixes both: per-stream loss recovery keeps unrelated streams flowing, and datagrams give the UDP-style semantics game state, live audio and telemetry actually want — without leaving the browser's security model. It also inherits QUIC connection migration, so a Wi-Fi-to-cellular switch keeps the session.

Today it's forward-looking, not a default. Browser support is real but uneven, middlebox and load-balancer support more so, and UDP on 443 is still blocked on plenty of corporate networks; the wire protocol is an IETF draft, not an RFC. The defensible position: WebSocket remains the answer for bidirectional browser traffic now, and WebTransport is what you reach for when unreliable delivery or independent streams matter enough to run HTTP/3 end to end and keep a fallback.

Where it matters: cloud gaming, live media, realtime telemetry, and any voice/AI path where a late audio frame is worse than a lost one. (→ Items 72, 74; HTTP/3 and QUIC in Section 6)
